c0669: Choose your legal structure with your accountant: LLC or S corp
c0672: An LLC separates personal and business liability and suits partners. An S corp election can cut self-employment tax once profit is steady; ask your accountant when it pays off.
c0673: Get your EIN from the IRS and register for state payroll and unemployment tax
c0676: The EIN is free and takes minutes online at irs.gov. Register with your state workforce agency before your first hire, so your payroll provider can file from day one.
c0677: File your LLC with the Secretary of State and appoint a registered agent
c0680: File the articles of organization and sign an operating agreement, even for a single-member LLC. Filing fees and processing times vary by state; check the state website.
c0681: Open a business bank account and keep finances separate
c0684: Bring your EIN letter and formation documents. Keep a card for purchases and a separate account for deposits, so event deposits never mix with personal money.
c0685: Get a seller's permit and register for state sales tax
c0688: In many states sales tax applies to the whole catering invoice: food, staff and rentals. Confirm your state's rule and whether service charges are taxed before you quote.
c0689: Apply for the city or county business license (and a DBA if you use a trade name)
c0692: Check every city where you plan to cater: some require a license to operate there. A DBA (fictitious business name) is filed with the county or state.
c0693: Hire an accountant or bookkeeper and set up quarterly estimated taxes
c0696: Ask for catering experience. Estimated taxes are due quarterly; put a share of every deposit into a tax savings account so the bill never surprises you.
c0697: Choose catering software for proposals, contracts, deposits and invoices
c0700: One tool should send the quote, collect the e-signature and take the deposit by card or ACH. Test it with a mock proposal before you pay for a full year.
c0701: Have an attorney draft your standard catering contract
c0704: Cover deposit, cancellation and postponement terms, guest minimum, final guest count date, and service charge versus gratuity. Reuse it for every event.
c0705: Write your HACCP-based food safety plan and transport SOPs
c0708: Document temperatures, cooling, reheating and hot and cold holding during transport. Your health department may ask for it at permit review.
c0709: Get your Certified Food Protection Manager certificate (ServSafe Manager)
c0712: Most health departments require one certified manager. Take an ANSI-accredited exam and keep a copy for your permit file and for every event binder.
c0718: Choose a shared commissary kitchen: hours, cold and dry storage, van parking
c0721: Visit at least three. Compare peak-hour availability, walk-in space, parking for the van and the deposit. Ask whether the health department has approved the kitchen for catering.
c0725: The health department requires it. It should name your hours, storage areas, parking and cleaning duties. Keep a copy for the permit application.
c0726: Apply for the county catering / health permit
c0729: Plan review applies mainly if you lease your own kitchen. Expect an application, a fee, a menu review and an inspection of the kitchen and the van.
c0730: Get temporary food event permits for community or public events
c0733: Your catering permit usually does not cover public or community events. Each event may need its own temporary food permit; apply well before the date.
c0734: Check fire marshal rules for open flame, chafing fuel and tents
c0737: Rules depend on the venue and the city. Ask venues about open flame, fuel canisters and cooking under tents, and keep fire extinguishers on the van.
c0738: Buy a used refrigerated cargo van and have it inspected
c0741: Get a mechanical inspection and test the refrigeration unit under load. Check mileage, service records and payload, and read the title for liens.
c0742: Register and title the van and buy commercial auto insurance
c0745: Register it in the business name. A CDL is needed only when the gross vehicle weight rating is 26,001 lb or more, which a standard cargo van is not.
c0746: Upfit the van: shelving, load restraints and branding
c0749: Add racks, tie-downs and non-slip liners so loads cannot shift. A wrap helps marketing, but check that your insurer covers the upfit.
c0750: Buy general liability and business owner's policy coverage, and order certificates of insurance
c0753: Venues and planners ask for a certificate of insurance (COI) naming them as additional insured. Ask your broker for same-day COIs.
c0754: Add liquor liability if you serve alcohol the client buys
c0757: Skip it if no alcohol is served at your events. If your bartenders pour client-supplied alcohol, you need liquor liability and certified bartenders.
c0758: Buy workers' compensation coverage before your first hire
c0761: Required in almost every state once you have employees, including part-time event staff. Premiums depend on payroll and class code.
c0762: Arrange waste and grease removal with a licensed hauler
c0765: The commissary often handles it. Confirm who removes grease and trash for the van and what you must label, store and log.
c0766: Arrange pest control with a licensed company and post required notices
c0769: Usually through the commissary. Keep service records and post the permit and any required notices where inspectors expect them.
c0772: List what you own versus what you rent for each service style
c0775: Drop-off, buffet, family-style, plated and stations need different equipment. Rent what you use rarely and buy what you use at nearly every event.
c0776: Buy chafing dishes, insulated carriers and calibrated thermometers
c0779: Choose insulated carriers that hold food hot or cold for the whole trip. Calibrate thermometers and keep spares in the van.
c0780: Buy portable cooking and power: induction, burners and a generator
c0783: Venues rarely have enough power for heavy cooking. Induction units are quiet and safer indoors; use a generator only where fire rules allow.
c0784: Stock hotel pans, sheet pans and utensils
c0787: Standardize on hotel pan sizes so everything stacks, travels and fits the carriers. Label pans and lids by station.
c0788: Buy serving and presentation pieces for chef-attended stations
c0791: Platters, risers, signage and a small tool kit per station. A consistent look is what makes your themed stations memorable in photos.
c0792: Open accounts with a broadline distributor (US Foods, Sysco, Restaurant Depot)
c0795: Compare delivery minimums, credit terms and price lists. Restaurant Depot works well for small orders; broadline accounts cut costs as volume grows.
c0796: Line up specialty suppliers for your themed stations
c0799: Think of tortillas, proteins for carving, fresh pasta, fish for poke. Get quotes and delivery days from at least two suppliers per item.
c0800: Sign an agreement with a party rental company for tables, linens and dinnerware
c0803: Negotiate a caterer rate and standard delivery and pickup times. Rentals are billed to the client, so build them into your proposal.
c0804: Choose disposables and packaging for drop-off orders
c0807: Use compostable items where your city requires them. Test that hot food stays hot and that lids do not leak in a moving van.
c0808: Set up temperature logging for transport with a data logger
c0811: Place a logger in each carrier and in the van's cargo area. Save the report after every event as proof that food stayed in the safe zone.
c0812: Set up your commissary space: shelving, labeling and FIFO
c0815: Label and date everything, and store first in, first out. Shared kitchens are inspected often, so a tidy, labeled space protects your permit.
c0816: Run a full dry run of an event with your team
c0819: Cook, pack, load, drive and set up for a mock event at a friend's venue. Time every step and fix what was slow before a client sees it.
c0822: Set a staffing plan per event by service style (servers per guest)
c0825: Buffets need fewer servers than plated dinners. Write a servers-per-guest ratio for each style and use it to price labor in every quote.
c0826: Build a pool of event staff on W-2 payroll, not 1099
c0829: Event servers and bartenders are usually employees, not contractors (FLSA economic reality test; California AB5). Misclassification brings back wages and penalties.
c0830: Prepare offer letters, I-9 and W-4 for each hire, and check state minimum wage
c0833: Complete Form I-9 within three business days of the start date and collect a W-4. Check state and local minimum wage and any minimum shift rules.
c0834: File new-hire reports with your state
c0837: Every state requires one, usually within 20 days. Most payroll providers file it for you automatically; confirm that yours does.
c0838: Set up a payroll provider and workers' comp on payroll
c0841: Connect payroll to your workers' comp policy so premiums follow actual hours. Set a clear pay schedule, including how event-night overtime is paid.
c0842: Get food handler cards for your whole team
c0845: Many states and counties require a food handler card for anyone handling food. Cards are cheap, online and valid for about 2-3 years.
c0846: Get alcohol server certification for your bartenders (TIPS, ServSafe Alcohol or TABC)
c0849: Required or strongly recommended where alcohol is served. Insurers often ask for it, and it is a selling point for planners and venues.
c0850: Cover OSHA basics: burns, lifting and driving safety
c0853: Train staff on hot pans, safe lifting and loading, and van driving. Keep an injury log and a first-aid kit in the van and at every event.
c0854: Train service and event protocol: uniform, briefing and the nine major allergens
c0857: Run a pre-event briefing every time. Everyone should know the nine major allergens and how to hand an allergy question to the chef.
c0858: Set your service charge and gratuity policy
c0861: A mandatory service charge is wages (IRS Rev. Rul. 2012-18); a gratuity is voluntary and goes to staff. Keep them on separate invoice lines and check your state's sales tax rule.
c0864: Create your brand, logo, themed station menu and professional photos
c0867: Photograph the stations, the plating and the team in action. Photos sell catering far better than menus, so invest here.
c0868: Build a website with menus, per-guest starting prices and a quote request form
c0871: Show packages by service style and a starting price per guest. A short form that asks for date, venue and guest count gets you better leads.
c0872: Set up your Google Business Profile and collect reviews
c0875: Pick the catering category and add your service area and photos. Ask every client for a review; local search brings many leads.
c0876: Create profiles on The Knot and WeddingWire
c0879: Both are the main directories for wedding clients. Upload photos, list packages and answer inquiries within a few hours.
c0880: Join ezCater to reach corporate clients
c0883: ezCater is a corporate catering marketplace that charges a commission on each order. Include that commission in your prices from the start.
c0884: Prospect corporate clients: office managers, HR and event planners
c0887: Build a list of nearby offices and drop off sample lunches. Repeat weekday orders make your base, so follow up every contact.
c0888: Make agreements with venues and wedding planners (preferred vendor lists)
c0891: Ask each venue how to join its preferred list. Offer a tasting for the planner; their referrals turn into weekend bookings.
c0892: Define your tasting policy for prospects
c0895: Decide who gets a tasting, how many guests attend and whether the fee is credited toward the booking. Track the bookings each tasting produces.
c0896: Post event photos on Instagram and social media
c0899: Share event photos with the client's permission. Use text or SMS for quick client follow-ups; keep inquiries in your CRM.
c0900: Create a proposal template with the kit calculator and track leads in your CRM
c0903: Your calculator gives the price per guest; the template turns it into a polished quote. Log every inquiry and follow up within 48 hours.
c0904: Start a referral and review program for after each event
c0907: Send a thank-you message with a review link a day after the event. Offer something small to clients who refer a friend or a company.
c0908: Host a launch event or showcase for planners and companies
c0911: Invite planners, venue managers and office managers to a tasting of your stations. It is your best single day of sales.
c0914: Hold the client briefing at D-21: guests, diets and event timeline
c0917: Confirm the guest count, dietary needs, service style, arrival time and who your contact is on the day. Send the summary in writing.
c0918: Visit the venue at D-14: access, kitchen, outlets and water
c0921: Check loading access, parking, elevator, power, water and fire rules. Photograph the space and note where stations and chafers will go.
c0922: Order ingredients at D-7 and D-1 and write the production list
c0925: Order against the final guest count and add a small buffer. Build one production list with prep times and who does what.
c0926: Complete the loading and transport checklist with temperatures
c0929: Check carriers, pans, equipment and rentals against the list. Record food temperatures when you load and again when you arrive.
c0930: Set up 60-90 minutes before service and run the event
c0933: Arrive early, set up the stations and check hot and cold temperatures before guests arrive. Brief staff, then keep a service timeline.
c0934: Pick up, clean and return rentals
c0936: Day of event or next morning
c0937: Count and inspect rentals before you leave. Return them clean by the agreed time to avoid late fees.
c0938: Invoice the balance and collect within 24-48 hours; track deposits
c0941: Send the final invoice right away, including any overages. Match deposits received against your quote and chase unpaid balances early.
c0942: Ask for a review and photos; follow up in your CRM
c0945: Thank the client, share a review link and ask permission to use photos. Note preferences for the next booking.
c0946: Review food cost and labor per event against the calculator every week
c0949: Compare actual food, staff hours and rentals with what the calculator projected. Small gaps add up quickly across a season.
c0950: Do your 90-day review: price per guest, guest minimums and packages
c0953: Look at which events earned the most, which took too long and which packages sold. Adjust prices, minimums and offers.
